title: Absorbing a split torus into a split-solvable torus complement
statement: Let $k$ be any field [def-weil-field]. Let $U$ be a smooth geometrically connected affine $k$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and assume $U$ is split unipotent: in a faithful finite-dimensional matrix representation all its geometric points are unipotent matrices, and it has a finite descending series $U=U_0\supset U_1\supset\cdots\supset U_m=1$ of smooth geometrically connected closed $k$-subgroups, each normal in its predecessor, whose fppf quotient sheaves $U_i/U_{i+1}$ are represented by $\mathbf G_{a,k}$ [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup, def-sc-gm-ga]. An fppf quotient sheaf means the sheafification of the right-coset functor for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings of commutative $k$-algebras. Let $D\simeq\mathbf G_{m,k}^r$ be a split torus, $r\geq0$, acting on $U$ by $k$-group automorphisms: a morphism $D\times_kU\to U$ satisfying the unit and action identities and preserving the group law of $U$. Form the semidirect product $H=U\rtimes D$, whose underlying scheme is $U\times_kD$ and whose multiplication on every algebra is $(u,d)(v,e)=(u(d\cdot v),de)$. For every closed split torus $T\subseteq H$ there is an element $u\in U(k)$ such that $uTu^{-1}\subseteq \{1\}\times_kD$ as closed subgroup schemes of $H$. A split torus here means a $k$-group isomorphic to $\mathbf G_{m,k}^s$ for some $s\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ and $\mathbf G_a(A)=(A,+)$. The asserted inclusion holds on points over every commutative $k$-algebra after scalar extension of $u$. No perfectness, infinitude or characteristic assumption is imposed.

source.place: Proposition 16.54 and its proof, printed p.344: maximal split tori of a split solvable group are images of sections of its split-torus quotient and are conjugate under the unipotent kernel. An arbitrary split torus lies in a maximal one by bounded dimension. Applied to H=U semidirect D; the torus D is a maximal split torus because the kernel is unipotent. This is the split-solvable assertion, not reductive-group rational conjugacy.

proof.text:
Choose a split-torus coordinate isomorphism $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^s$ and write its inclusion in $H=U\rtimes D$ as $t\mapsto(c(t),a(t))$. Projection to $D$ is a homomorphism, so $a:T\to D$ is a homomorphism. Multiplication in $H$ gives, on every algebra,
$$c(tt')=c(t)\bigl(a(t)\cdot c(t')\bigr).$$
Thus $c:T\to U$ is a scheme morphism satisfying this crossed-homomorphism identity for the $T$-action $t\cdot v=a(t)\cdot v$. This action is by group automorphisms, by the action identities for $D$ and the homomorphism identity for $a$.

source.place: Example 15.1, printed pp.302–303, and the opening observation of Theorem 16.27, p.333; coordinate form of the given inclusion.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-split-unipotent-torus-stable-series] to this $T$-action on $U$. Its hypotheses are precisely the given smooth, geometrically connected, affine, finite-type split-unipotent $U$, and the split torus $T$ just identified with $\mathbf G_m^s$. Obtain $U=V_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq V_m=1$, quotient homomorphisms $q_i:V_i\to\mathbf G_a$ with kernel $V_{i+1}$, and monomial characters $\chi_i(t)=t^{n_i}$ describing the $T$-action. The tail beginning at $V_{i+1}$ is a split additive series for $V_{i+1}$. No assertion that an arbitrary subgroup of a split unipotent group is split is being used.

source.place: Summary 16.29(d), printed p.334, and Proposition 16.54, p.344; the equivariant structural input is stated separately, with its arbitrary-field scope.

proof.text:
For later use, if a morphism $f:\mathbf G_m^s\to\mathbf G_a$ satisfies $f(tt')=f(t)+t^n f(t')$, write its Laurent polynomial as $f(X)=\sum_{a\in\mathbf Z^s}\lambda_aX^a$ with finite support. The identity in $k[X_1^{\pm1},\ldots,X_s^{\pm1},Y_1^{\pm1},\ldots,Y_s^{\pm1}]$ is
$$\sum_a\lambda_aX^aY^a=\sum_a\lambda_aX^a+X^n\sum_a\lambda_aY^a.$$
For $a\ne0$, comparing coefficients of $Y^a$ gives $\lambda_aX^a=\lambda_aX^n$, hence $\lambda_a=0$ unless $a=n$. Also $f(1)=0$. If $n\ne0$, it follows that $f(X)=b(1-X^n)$ for $b=\lambda_0\in k$; if $n=0$, only the constant term can occur and it is zero, so take $b=0$. This includes $s=0$. These are coordinate-ring identities and therefore hold on all test algebras, including nonreduced ones.

source.place: Proposition 15.3, printed pp.305–306, scalar crossed-homomorphism calculation; the Laurent-coefficient argument here is supplied by the worker and works over any field.

proof.text: For each $b\in k$, the fibre $P=q_i^{-1}(b)$ is a represented right $V_{i+1}$-torsor over $\operatorname{Spec}k$. Indeed [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] applied to the normal inclusion $V_{i+1}\subseteq V_i$ identifies its quotient with $\mathbf G_a$ by the isomorphism $b_i$ furnished in step 2, gives a faithfully flat finitely presented quotient map, and gives the torsor isomorphism $(v,w)\mapsto(v,vw)$. Restricting this isomorphism to the fibre gives $P\times_kV_{i+1}\simeq P\times_kP$; [lem-trf-fppf-covering-base-change] applied to the singleton quotient cover gives flatness, local finite presentation and surjectivity of $P\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, and [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-morphism-permanence](3) gives finite presentation by base change from $q_i$. All groups in this normal inclusion are affine and finite type. The kernel $V_{i+1}$ is smooth and connected and has the split additive tail series from step 2. Apply [lem-sfb-split-unipotent-affine-torsor-section] with the affine finite-type base $\operatorname{Spec}k$ to obtain $v\in P(k)$. Consequently every $b\in k$ has a lift $v\in V_i(k)$ with $q_i(v)=b$.

source.place: Proposition 16.55(b), printed p.344; quotient torsor of Corollary 5.27, p.105, pulled back to a rational point. The fibre restriction is the explicit base change of the quotient torsor. Stacks Tag 021O (topologies.tex, lemma-fppf (3)) for the base-changed fppf cover; finite-presentation base change as in the cited permanence node.

proof.text:
Induct on $i=0,\ldots,m$ with the claim that some $w_i\in U(k)$ makes $\operatorname{Int}(w_i^{-1})$ carry the given inclusion to $t\mapsto(c_i(t),a(t))$ with $c_i:T\to V_i$. Take $w_0=1$, $c_0=c$. Assume this holds at $i<m$. Since the conjugated map is a homomorphism, $c_i$ has the crossed identity from step 1. Equivariance and additivity of $q_i$ imply that $f_i=q_i c_i$ satisfies $f_i(tt')=f_i(t)+\chi_i(t)f_i(t')$. Step 3 gives $b\in k$ with $f_i(t)=b-\chi_i(t)b$, and step 4 lifts $b$ to $v\in V_i(k)$. Put $w_{i+1}=w_iv$. Direct multiplication gives
$$c_{i+1}(t)=v^{-1}c_i(t)(a(t)\cdot v),\qquad q_i(c_{i+1}(t))=-b+f_i(t)+\chi_i(t)b=0.$$
All three factors belong to $V_i$ because it is $T$-stable. The scheme-theoretic kernel identity $\ker q_i=V_{i+1}$ factors this morphism through $V_{i+1}$. This proves the induction, with the displayed identities on every algebra.

source.place: Theorem 16.27(a), printed p.333, successive removal of principal crossed homomorphisms, in the split-kernel case of Summary 16.29(d), p.334; explicit induction and conjugation sign.

proof.text: At $i=m$, $V_m=1$, so $c_m(t)=1$ on every algebra. Thus $w_m^{-1}Tw_m$ factors through the closed subgroup $\{1\}\times_kD$. Taking $u=w_m^{-1}\in U(k)$ gives the claimed subgroup-scheme inclusion: for every $k$-algebra $A$ and $t\in T(A)$ the conjugate equals $(1,a_A(t))$. When $U=1$ the induction has no steps and $u=1$; when $T=1$ it gives the same conclusion. The argument uses no injection or surjectivity assertion about $a:T\to D$, no rational density, and no assumption on the field beyond the stated hypotheses.
